*(Part (i) of this sub-question is on a page missing from the scanned paper and is not transcribed.)*

(ii) Arrange the group VII elements in order of increasing oxidizing strength.

Explain the trend.

(iii) Write balanced chemical equations to show the reactions of $\mathrm{Cl_{2(g)}}$ with

A) Cold dilute KOH

B) Hot concentrated KOH.

(iv) Give the formulae and names of the oxo-acids of iodine in the following oxidation states:

| Oxidation state | Formula | Name |
|---|---|---|
| +1 | | |
| +5 | | |

*[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(ii) Order of increasing oxidising strength:** $\mathrm{I_2} < \mathrm{Br_2} < \mathrm{Cl_2} < \mathrm{F_2}$.

**Explanation.** Oxidising strength is the tendency of the halogen to **gain electrons**: $\mathrm{X_2} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{X^-}$. Going **down the group** the atoms get larger and the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded by the inner shells, so the nucleus attracts the incoming electron less strongly; the halide ion is also bigger and is hydrated less strongly. The reaction $\mathrm{X_2} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{X^-}$ becomes less favourable, and the standard electrode potentials become less positive: $\mathrm{F_2}$ $+2.87\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ $+1.36\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Br_2}$ $+1.07\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{I_2}$ $+0.54\ \mathrm{V}$. Evidence: a halogen displaces a less oxidising halogen from its halide, for example $\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{Br^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^-} + \mathrm{Br_2}$.

**(iii) Reactions of chlorine with potassium hydroxide (disproportionation).**

A) Cold dilute KOH: $\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{KClO} + \mathrm{H_2O}$ (potassium chlorate(I), hypochlorite; chlorine goes from 0 to $-1$ and $+1$).

B) Hot concentrated KOH: $3\mathrm{Cl_2} + 6\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{KClO_3} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}$ (potassium chlorate(V); chlorine goes from 0 to $-1$ and $+5$).

Atom check for B: left K 6, Cl 6, O 6, H 6; right K $5 + 1 = 6$, Cl $5 + 1 = 6$, O $3 + 3 = 6$, H 6.

**(iv) Oxo-acids of iodine.**

| Oxidation state | Formula | Name |
|---|---|---|
| +1 | $\mathrm{HIO}$ (also written $\mathrm{HOI}$) | iodic(I) acid (hypoiodous acid) |
| +5 | $\mathrm{HIO_3}$ | iodic(V) acid (iodic acid) |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) How does the second ionization energy vary for group I and group II elements in the same period of the Periodic Table.

Give a reason for your trend

(ii) Lithium shows a diagonal relationship with magnesium.

A) Why are these elements diagonally related?

B) Give one reaction in which Li and Mg show a diagonal relationship.

(iii) With the use of chemical equations show the effect of heat on the nitrates of lithium and potassium.

$\mathrm{LiNO_3}$

$\mathrm{KNO_3}$

(iv) How does the solubility of hydroxides of the group II elements vary down the group?. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trend.** In the same period the **second ionisation energy of a group I element is much larger than that of the group II element**. Examples ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$): Li $7298$ against Be $1757$; Na $4562$ against Mg $1451$.

**Reason.** After losing one electron a group I atom has the stable noble-gas configuration (for example $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $2.8$). The second electron must be removed from a **full inner shell, closer to the nucleus and only weakly shielded**, so it is held very strongly and a very large energy is needed. A group II atom, after losing one electron, still has one electron in its **outer s sub-shell** ($\mathrm{Mg^+}$, $2.8.1$); this electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by the inner shells, so it is removed far more easily.

**(ii) Diagonal relationship.**

A) Going across a period the charge of the ion increases (for example $\mathrm{Li^+}$ to $\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$), while going down a group the ionic radius increases (for example $\mathrm{Li^+}$ to $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$ to $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$). The diagonal neighbours lithium and magnesium therefore have a **similar charge-to-size ratio (charge density)**, hence similar **polarising power** and electronegativity, and so similar properties, unlike the other members of their own groups.

B) One reaction (any of the following):

- Both burn in nitrogen to form nitrides: $6\mathrm{Li} + \mathrm{N_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_3N}$ and $3\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{N_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg_3N_2}$ (no other group I metal does this directly);
- both burn in oxygen to give the normal oxide ($\mathrm{Li_2O}$, $\mathrm{MgO}$) and not a peroxide;
- both nitrates decompose on heating to the oxide, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$.

**(iii) Effect of heat on the nitrates.**

$\mathrm{LiNO_3}$: lithium nitrate decomposes to the oxide: $4\mathrm{LiNO_3} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_2O} + 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$ (the small $\mathrm{Li^+}$ ion polarises the nitrate ion strongly).

$\mathrm{KNO_3}$: potassium nitrate only loses oxygen and gives the nitrite: $2\mathrm{KNO_3} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KNO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$.

**(iv) Solubility of the group II hydroxides.** The solubility **increases down the group**: $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ is almost insoluble, $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ is sparingly soluble (lime water), $\mathrm{Sr(OH)_2}$ is more soluble and $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ is quite soluble.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) In the space below sketch a graph of variation of the first ionization energy for the elements Sodium to Argon.

(ii) In Complete the table below giving the formulae of the oxides of the elements

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula of stable oxide | | | | | | |

(iii) From the list of oxides in c (ii) select an oxide which is likely to be:

Amphoteric:

Neutral:

Acidic: *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sketch of the first ionisation energy, Na to Ar.** Plot first ionisation energy (vertical axis, $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) against the element (horizontal axis, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar). Approximate values to plot:

| Element | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First ionisation energy ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) | 496 | 738 | 578 | 786 | 1012 | 1000 | 1251 | 1521 |

Shape of the graph: **a general rise from Na (lowest) to Ar (highest)**, because the nuclear charge increases across the period while the shielding stays the same and the atomic radius decreases. There are **two small dips**: Al is lower than Mg (the 3p electron of Al is higher in energy and slightly shielded by the 3s electrons) and S is lower than P (in S two electrons share a 3p orbital and repel each other, so one is removed more easily). The graph rises, falls at Al, rises to P, falls slightly at S, then rises to a maximum at Ar.

**(ii) Formulae of the stable oxides.**

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula of stable oxide | $\mathrm{Li_2O}$ | $\mathrm{BeO}$ | $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$ | $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (also $\mathrm{CO}$) | $\mathrm{NO_2}$ (also $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{NO}$) | $\mathrm{OF_2}$ |

(Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so its compound with oxygen, $\mathrm{OF_2}$, is strictly a fluoride of oxygen.)

**(iii) Choice from the oxides listed.**

- Amphoteric: $\mathrm{BeO}$ (reacts with both acids and strong bases, giving $\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{[Be(OH)_4]^{2-}}$).
- Neutral: $\mathrm{CO}$ (or $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{NO}$): no reaction with water, acids or bases.
- Acidic: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (or $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$, $\mathrm{NO_2}$, $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$): non-metal oxides that react with water or alkali to give acids or salts.
